To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the disability rating used in California's workers' Compensation program is not a good predictor of lost earnings and that the severity of impairment varies considerably across different upper extremity injuries.

the labor market impact of permanent disability due to upper extremity musculok skeletal injuries varies considerably across injuries and that the severity of disability ratings does not predict this impact.

(1) workers with musculoskeletal injuries of the shoulder have larger earnings losses than workers with injuries of the wrist or elbow; and (2) disability ratings are poor predictors of the severity of earnings losses.

the economic consequences of permanent musculoskeletal disability, with a focus on the labor market consequences.
the labor market consequences of musculoskeletal injuries to the upper extremity.
understanding the economic impact of upper extremities injuries on the labor market.

the severity of impairment for different upper extremity injuries is not well captured by the disability ratings that are used to determine compensation.
there are significant earnings losses for workers with musculoskeletal injuries to the upper extremity.
upper extremity musculo skeletal injury is costly to the economy, and that current methods of rating disability do not adequately capture the costs of different types of injuries.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the disability rating does not predict well the impact of upper extremities injuries on labor market outcomes.
the disability ratings used by California are not good predictors of labor market outcomes for injured workers.
there is a need for a more comprehensive measure of impairment that takes into account the labor market experience of the injured worker.

there is a large gap between the severity of the disability rating and the severity of the injury.
